concept: Oplog capacity for initial sync, live migration and bulk loads
summary: Source-anchored research for Oplog capacity for initial sync, live migration and bulk loads. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Logical initial sync buffers newly added source oplog records in a temporary collection in the destination's local database during the data copy, then applies them. Buffering does not remove source retention requirements: the source oplog window must be long enough for the destination to fetch new entries between the start and end of the logical initial sync, and a continuity gap restarts the initial sync. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-sync.md

Monitor the oplog time window alongside migration lag throughout the migration. MongoDB mongosync and Percona ClusterSync both document comparing db.getReplicationInfo().timeDiff with their respective lag metrics and increasing retention when lag approaches the window. (medium confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/oplog-sizing.md ; https://docs.percona.com/percona-clustersync-for-mongodb/oplog-sizing.html

Increasing retained history gives more catch-up time but is a separate lever from sync speed. When lag remains high, mongosync docs recommend scaling up the mongosync node (CPU or memory) for a higher copy rate. Percona ClusterSync docs recommend running PCSM closer to the destination, adding CPU and memory on the PCSM host, and using faster destination hardware for write performance. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/oplog-sizing.md ; https://docs.percona.com/percona-clustersync-for-mongodb/oplog-sizing.html

A June 2, 2025 Percona community incident report describes a mongosync bulk load causing a destination shard secondary to lag beyond retained oplog history and remain unhealthy. This is an anecdotal failure report, not a controlled benchmark or a reason to copy its destructive recovery commands. (low confidence)

For Percona ClusterSync, larger queues absorb temporary bursts but do not fix a destination that is permanently slower than the source. Its October 1, 2026 engineering guidance recommends tuning clone and replication concurrency against available CPU and disk capacity; retention headroom alone cannot create sustained apply throughput. (low confidence)

For change-stream-based mongosync and Percona ClusterSync migrations, required changes must remain available in source oplog history. If required operations expire before the migration processes them, synchronization fails; large clones and pauses increase the retention risk. (medium confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/oplog-sizing.md ; https://docs.percona.com/percona-clustersync-for-mongodb/oplog-sizing.html

The oplog window is the time between the newest and oldest oplog entries, so it depends on workload rather than being fixed by the oplog's configured size. The oplog window and replication lag may vary during a migration, so monitor them repeatedly during the migration. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-oplog.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/oplog-sizing.md

mongosync consumes change streams rather than reading the source oplog directly, but its historical events must remain inside the source oplog time range. Its sizing guide says synchronization fails if required unapplied operations roll off the source oplog. (low confidence)

AWS DMS guidance for migration to DocumentDB explicitly requires the source to retain ongoing changes until full load completes for every included collection. For a MongoDB source, size its oplog to hold operations generated during full load. Treat this as DMS-specific guidance rather than a universal model for native replica-set initial sync. (low confidence)

Bulk maintenance and ingestion planning must account for write history rather than net database growth: multi-document updates expand into individual oplog operations, roughly balanced inserts and deletes can generate a large oplog, and in-place updates can generate history without increasing stored data size. (low confidence)

Minimum retention is a time constraint rather than a strict disk cap: MongoDB removes an entry only after both the configured oplog size is reached and the entry exceeds the minimum age. Budget disk headroom when increasing the retention period. (low confidence)

Logical replica-set initial sync fetches new oplog records during collection cloning and index building, stores them in a temporary collection in the destination local database, and applies buffered records afterward. Provision disk for that temporary history; source oplog bytes alone do not cover this destination requirement. (high confidence)

For a sharded mongosync migration, measure db.getReplicationInfo().timeDiff on each shard and compare the smallest window with lag.overallLagSeconds from /progress. Repeat during migration; if lag approaches that minimum, increase retention or improve migration throughput. (low confidence)

Plan destination oplog storage separately from source retention. mongosync initial copying generates destination insert oplog entries, and logical initial sync also needs local storage for buffered history; data size alone is therefore insufficient for disk planning. (high confidence) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/oplog-sizing.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/manual/core/replica-set-sync.md

Cloud Manager Agent push live migration can buffer the initial-sync oplog window to a configured disk directory. The migration host must have enough storage in that directory for the buffered oplog. This is an agent migration behavior, not a universal mongosync setting. (low confidence)

During logical initial sync catch-up, MongoDB checks continuity against the source. A gap requires restarting initial sync. The documented source window requirement includes the buffered-oplog application and final catch-up phases, with additional time for changing conditions. (low confidence)

Plan destination storage for both the migrated dataset and the destination oplog generated by applied writes. Retention on the source and free space on the destination are separate capacity requirements. (medium confidence)
